note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Definition and Types of Companies
explain: A company is an entity incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or any previous company law.
Company limited by shares restricts member liability to unpaid share amounts.
Company limited by guarantee restricts liability to the amount undertaken in the memorandum upon winding up.
Private company restricts share transfers and limits member count to 200 (excluding employees).
Public company is not a private company and has no ceiling on maximum members.
Small company has paid-up capital not exceeding ₹4 crore and turnover not exceeding ₹40 crore.
One Person Company (OPC) is a private company with only one individual member.
Government company has at least 51% paid-up share capital held by Central or State Governments.
Foreign company is incorporated outside India but has a place of business or activity in India.

flow.title: Determining Company Classification
steps: Check incorporation place inside or outside India
Identify member count and share transferability
Verify capital and turnover for small status
Check Government shareholding percentage

topics.example: A company with 5 members and ₹2 crore capital where Central Govt owns 55% is a Government Public Company.
remember: Small Company limits: Capital ≤ ₹4 crore and Turnover ≤ ₹40 crore.
Private company max members: 200 (joint holders count as 1).
mistakes: Counting current or former employee-members in the 200-member ceiling for private companies.
Treating a subsidiary of a public company as a private company just because its articles say so.

quiz.q: What is the maximum turnover threshold for a company to qualify as a 'Small Company'?
quiz.why: As per the updated rules under Section 2(85), the turnover limit for a small company is ₹40 crore.

quiz.q: A private company has 2 joint holders of 50 shares. How are they counted towards the 200-member limit?
quiz.why: Joint holders of shares are treated as a single member under Section 2(68).

topics.title: Maintenance of Books of Account
explain: Every company must prepare and keep books of account at its registered office.
Books must be maintained on accrual basis and double-entry system of accounting.
Board of Directors can decide to keep books at another place by informing ROC within 7 days.
Branch offices must keep proper books and send periodic summarized returns to registered office.
Accounting software must feature an unalterable audit trail recording every transaction and edit log from April 1, 2022.
Company books and relevant vouchers must be preserved in good order for at least 8 financial years.

flow.title: Process of Maintaining Books of Account
steps: Record transactions on accrual and double entry
Keep books at registered office by default
File ROC notice in 7 days if moved
Maintain accounting software with audit trail
Back up electronic data daily in India
Retain books for minimum 8 years

topics.example: If a business moves its accounting department from Mumbai HQ to Pune branch, it must file notice with ROC within 7 days.
remember: Notice to ROC for non-registered office location: within 7 days.
Retention period for books of account: minimum 8 financial years.
Daily electronic backup must be stored on servers located physically in India.
mistakes: Thinking audit trail feature in accounting software can be temporarily disabled.
Assuming branch returns only need to be sent once a year instead of periodically.

quiz.q: Within how many days must a company notify the ROC if books of account are kept at a place other than the registered office?
quiz.why: Section 128 requires informing the Registrar of Companies within 7 days of the Board's decision.

quiz.q: For how long must a company preserve its books of account in good order?
quiz.why: Section 128(5) mandates retaining books of account for at least 8 financial years.

topics.title: Statutory Books and Registers
explain: Companies are legally required to maintain specific statutory registers under different provisions of the Act.
Register of Investments held in own name (Sec 187) and Register of Charges (Sec 85).
Register of Members and Register of Debenture-holders (Sec 88).
Minute Books for general and board meetings (Sec 118).
Register of Contracts/Arrangements in which directors are interested (Sec 189).
Register of Directors and Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) and their shareholdings (Sec 170).
Register of Loans and Investments by Company (Sec 186).
Statistical books (like Share Application, Call, Transfer, and Dividend books) keep track of share-related activities.

flow.title: Statutory Record Keeping Workflow
steps: Execute corporate transaction or meeting
Update specific statutory register under relevant section
Maintain statistical records for share issues
Keep registers available for statutory inspection

topics.example: When a company issues debentures, details of debenture holders must be recorded in the Register of Security Holders under Sec 88.
remember: Minutes of meetings must be recorded in Minute Books under Sec 118.
Register of Directors and KMP shareholding is governed by Sec 170.
mistakes: Confusing statistical books (like Share Call Book) with mandatory statutory registers.
Forgetting to record director's interest in contracts in the Section 189 register.

quiz.q: Which section of Companies Act, 2013 governs the maintenance of Register of Members?
quiz.why: Section 88 lays down the requirement to maintain the Register of Members and other security holders.

quiz.q: Which of the following is considered a statistical book rather than a statutory register?
quiz.why: Share Transfer Book is a statistical book maintained for internal administration of share movements.

topics.title: Annual Return and Final Accounts Overview
explain: Every company must prepare an Annual Return (Sec 92) signed by a director and company secretary.
For OPC and Small Companies, the annual return can be signed by a CS alone or a director if there is no CS.
Annual Return must be filed with the ROC within 60 days of the AGM.
Board of Directors must present financial statements at every AGM (Sec 129).
Financial Statements (Sec 2(40)) comprise: Balance Sheet, Profit & Loss Account, Cash Flow Statement, Statement of Changes in Equity (if applicable), and Explanatory Notes.
OPC, Small Companies, Dormant Companies, and private start-ups are exempt from presenting a Cash Flow Statement.

flow.title: Final Accounts and Annual Return Process
steps: Prepare financial statements at year end
Board approves and signs financial statements
Present financial statements to AGM
Sign Annual Return via Director and CS
File Annual Return with ROC within 60 days

topics.example: A registered start-up private company prepares its annual financial statements including Balance Sheet and P&L but omits the Cash Flow statement legally.
remember: Filing deadline for Annual Return: 60 days from AGM date.
Cash Flow Statement exemption applies to OPC, Small Companies, Dormant Companies, and Start-up Private Companies.
mistakes: Assuming all private companies are exempt from preparing Cash Flow Statements (only small/start-up private companies are exempt).
Counting 30 days instead of 60 days for filing the Annual Return with ROC.

quiz.q: What is the time limit for filing the Annual Return with ROC after the AGM is held?
quiz.why: Section 92 mandates filing the annual return within 60 days from the date of the AGM.

quiz.q: Which entity is NOT exempt from mandatory inclusion of Cash Flow Statement in financial statements?
quiz.why: Public limited companies must include a Cash Flow Statement under Section 2(40).

topics.title: Schedule III Applicability and Accounting Standard Compliance
explain: Financial statements must comply with Accounting Standards notified under Section 133 and present a true and fair view.
If a specific governing Act prescribes a format (e.g., Insurance, Banking, Electricity), that specific format applies instead.
Schedule III Division I applies to companies following AS (Companies Accounting Standards Rules).
Schedule III Division II applies to companies following Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS).
Schedule III Division III applies to Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) following Ind AS.
Schedule III gives general instructions for presentation of Balance Sheet (Part I) and Statement of Profit and Loss (Part II).

flow.title: Selecting Applicable Schedule III Format
steps: Check if company governed by specific Act
If yes, follow specific statutory format
If no, check applicable accounting framework
Use Division I for AS companies
Use Division II for Ind AS non-NBFCs
Use Division III for Ind AS NBFCs

topics.example: A commercial bank follows Banking Regulation Act formats, while a manufacturing company applying AS uses Division I of Schedule III.
remember: Division I = Companies using AS.
Division II = Non-NBFCs using Ind AS.
Division III = NBFCs using Ind AS.
mistakes: Applying general Schedule III formats to Banking or Insurance companies governed by specific statutes.
Mixing AS disclosures with Ind AS framework rules.

quiz.q: Which Division of Schedule III applies to an NBFC required to follow Ind AS?
quiz.why: Division III of Schedule III is specifically prescribed for NBFCs applying Ind AS.

quiz.q: Mandatory compliance with Accounting Standards by companies is enforced under which section?
quiz.why: Section 133 mandates compliance with Accounting Standards notified by the Central Government.

topics.title: Key Financial Statement Disclosures and Classifications
explain: Debit balance of Profit and Loss is shown as a negative figure under 'Surplus' in Reserves & Surplus.
Even if overall Reserves and Surplus becomes negative, it is shown on the face of Balance Sheet under Reserves & Surplus.
Work in Process (WIP) opening and closing absolute balances are not required in P&L, only 'Changes in Inventories' are disclosed.
Current maturities of long-term debt must be classified under 'Short-Term Borrowings'.
Bonus shares issued in the last 5 years must be disclosed in Notes without requiring disclosure of source.
Trade Receivables are split into Non-Current and Current, and further sub-classified into Secured, Unsecured, and Doubtful with an Ageing Schedule.

flow.title: Classification of Balance Sheet Items
steps: Identify item nature and settlement horizon
Separate into Current vs Non-Current
Classify debt due within 12 months as Short-Term Borrowings
Adjust negative P&L balance inside Reserves & Surplus
Provide mandatory ageing schedules in Notes

topics.example: A 5-year bank loan repaid in 10 half-yearly installments of ₹1 lakh: 2 installments due within 12 months (₹2 lakh) go to Short-Term Borrowings, and 8 installments (₹8 lakh) to Long-Term Borrowings.
remember: Negative Reserves & Surplus balance stays under Shareholders' Funds on the Liabilities side.
Current maturity of long-term borrowing = Short-Term Borrowing.
mistakes: Showing negative Reserves & Surplus balance on the Assets side of the Balance Sheet.
Classifying current maturity of long-term debt under Other Current Liabilities instead of Short-Term Borrowings.

quiz.q: Where should a net negative balance of Reserves and Surplus be presented in the Balance Sheet?
o: As an asset under Non-Current Assets
As an asset under Current Assets
As a negative figure under Shareholders' Funds
quiz.why: Schedule III requires negative surplus/reserves to be presented under the head 'Reserves and Surplus' under Shareholders' Funds.

quiz.q: How should installments of long-term loans due within 12 months of the balance sheet date be classified?
quiz.why: As per amended Schedule III, current maturities of long-term debt are classified under Short-Term Borrowings.

topics.title: Meaning of Dividend and Sources of Declaration
explain: Dividend includes any interim dividend paid during the financial year.
Dividend can only be declared out of current year profits, undistributed past profits, or government guarantee funds.
Current and past year depreciation must be fully provided under Schedule II before declaring dividend.
Dividends cannot be paid out of capital under any circumstances.
Board of Directors may declare interim dividend out of profit & loss surplus or current financial year profits.
If loss is incurred in current year up to the preceding quarter, interim dividend rate cannot exceed average dividend rate of preceding 3 financial years.

flow.title: Checklist for Dividend Declaration
steps: Calculate current year profit
Deduct current and arrear depreciation under Schedule II
Set off carried-forward past losses
Select source: Current profits, past profits, or reserves
Confirm Board recommendation and declare dividend

topics.example: A company with current profit of ₹10 lakh must first deduct ₹2 lakh past depreciation and ₹3 lakh past losses before declaring dividend.
remember: Depreciation provision under Schedule II is mandatory before dividend declaration.
Interim dividend cap during current loss period: average rate of past 3 years.
mistakes: Declaring dividend without setting off carried-over previous losses or unprovided depreciation.
Paying dividend out of share capital.

quiz.q: Does the term 'Dividend' under Section 2(35) of the Companies Act include interim dividend?
o: Only if approved by shareholders in AGM
Only if declared from free reserves
quiz.why: Section 2(35) explicitly states that 'Dividend' includes any interim dividend.

quiz.q: If a company incurs loss up to the quarter before declaring interim dividend, what is the maximum permissible dividend rate?
o: Average dividend rate of immediately preceding 3 financial years
quiz.why: Section 123(3) caps interim dividend at the average rate of dividends declared in the preceding 3 financial years.

topics.title: Declaration of Dividend Out of Free Reserves
explain: When profits are inadequate, dividend can be declared out of free reserves subject to strict conditions.
Condition 1: Rate of dividend shall not exceed the average rate of dividend of the past 3 years (does not apply if no dividend was declared in all 3 years).
Condition 2: Total amount drawn from accumulated profits shall not exceed 10% (1/10th) of (Paid-up Capital + Free Reserves) as per latest audited BS.
Condition 3: Amount drawn must first be used to set off losses incurred in the financial year in which dividend is declared.
Condition 4: Balance of reserves after withdrawal must not fall below 15% of paid-up share capital.
Dividends can only be drawn from free reserves, not capital reserves or revaluation reserves.

flow.title: 4-Condition Rule Test for Dividend from Reserves
steps: Test 1: Check rate <= avg rate of past 3 years
Test 2: Check total drawal <= 10% of (Capital + Free Reserves)
Test 3: Apply drawn amount to absorb current year loss
Test 4: Ensure remaining reserves >= 15% of Paid-up Capital
Determine maximum allowable withdrawal amount

topics.example: Company has Capital = ₹80L, Free Reserve = ₹25L. Max drawal under Condition 2 is 10% of (80+25) = ₹10.5L. Remaining reserve after drawal must remain at least 15% of ₹80L = ₹12L.
remember: Max drawal cap: 10% of (Paid-up Capital + Free Reserves).
Minimum balance in reserves: 15% of Paid-up Capital.
Revaluation and Capital Reserves CANNOT be used.
mistakes: Including Revaluation Reserves or Capital Reserves while calculating free reserves.
Forgetting to set off current year loss before determining net dividend amount for equity shares.

quiz.q: What is the maximum amount a company can draw from accumulated free reserves to declare dividend?
quiz.why: Rule 2 of Dividend Rules 2014 caps the total withdrawal at 10% of the sum of paid-up share capital and free reserves.

quiz.q: After drawing from free reserves for dividend payment, the balance of reserves must not fall below:
quiz.why: Rule 4 of Dividend Rules 2014 requires remaining reserves to be at least 15% of paid-up share capital.

topics.title: Unpaid Dividend Account and IEPF Transfer
explain: Declared dividend must be deposited in a separate bank account within 5 days of declaration.
If dividend is unpaid or unclaimed after 30 days from declaration, company must transfer it to 'Unpaid Dividend Account' within 7 days.
If company defaults in transfer, it must pay interest @ 12% p.a. on the delayed amount for members' benefit.
Within 90 days of transfer, details of unpaid shareholders must be posted on the company website.
Money remaining unpaid/unclaimed in Unpaid Dividend Account for 7 years must be transferred to Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF).
All underlying shares in respect of which dividend was unpaid for 7 consecutive years must also be transferred to IEPF.

flow.title: Timeline of Unpaid Dividend Handling
steps: Day 0: Declare dividend
Day 5: Deposit dividend in separate bank account
Day 30: Expiry of payment window to shareholders
Day 37: Transfer unpaid dividend to Unpaid Dividend Account
Day 127: Upload unpaid list on company website
Year 7: Transfer unclaimed funds and shares to IEPF

topics.example: Dividend declared on 1st May remained unclaimed by 10 shareholders on 31st May. Company must transfer this total unclaimed amount to the Unpaid Dividend Account by 7th June.
remember: Deposit in separate bank account: within 5 days of declaration.
Transfer to Unpaid Dividend Account: within 7 days after 30 days.
Interest rate for delay: 12% per annum.
Transfer to IEPF: after 7 years.
mistakes: Counting 7 years from the date of dividend declaration instead of date of transfer to Unpaid Dividend Account.
Thinking transferred shares in IEPF cannot be claimed back by the rightful owner.

quiz.q: Within how many days from the date of dividend declaration must the amount be deposited in a scheduled bank?
quiz.why: Section 123(4) mandates depositing declared dividend in a separate bank account within 5 days.

quiz.q: What interest rate is charged if a company fails to transfer unpaid dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account on time?
quiz.why: Section 124(3) prescribes an interest penalty of 12% per annum for default in transferring unpaid dividend.
